analysis.one_liner: Bans health plans from imposing lifetime benefit caps below $5 million, rising over time.
analysis.headline: The bill never moved beyond its Senate committee referral and died when the 110th Congress ended, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop employer health plans and their insurers from putting a dollar limit on how much they will pay for a person's medical care over a lifetime — at least $5 million for the first two years, $10 million in years three and four, then rising with inflation. Plans at very small employers (fewer than 20 workers) would be exempt unless the employer asks for the protection. It would also order a study of how many people have been cut off by such caps. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people with employer health coverage who face a catastrophic illness or injury — cancer, organ transplant, premature birth, long hospitalizations — where medical bills can exhaust a plan's lifetime cap and leave them paying out of pocket or going uninsured. The cap mainly protects people who were already insured; when it runs out, coverage effectively ends mid-treatment. Very small employers gain flexibility to opt in or out.

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans and insurers from imposing aggregate lifetime benefit limits below $5 million in the first two plan years, $10 million in the third and fourth years, and higher inflation-adjusted amounts after that [S2] [S3].
Exempts plans at employers with fewer than 20 employees unless the employer requests the same limit, an attempt to avoid raising costs for the smallest firms [S2] [S3].
Requires the Institute of Medicine to study how many people reach the new lifetime limits, giving Congress data on how many patients exhaust their coverage [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and health insurers who offer group coverage would bear higher expected claims costs for enrollees with very expensive conditions, and those costs could flow into premiums for employers and workers. Very small employers are exempt unless they opt in.

drawbacks.text: The bill acknowledges a real cost: it exempts small employers (fewer than 20 employees) entirely, recognizing that higher minimum lifetime limits could raise premiums for small firms [S2] [S3].

A higher floor on lifetime benefits would raise expected claims for insurers and self-insured employers, costs likely passed through to premiums paid partly by workers; the bill provides no estimate of that cost increase [S3].

The bill addresses only lifetime dollar caps in the group market; it does nothing about annual limits, exclusions for pre-existing conditions, or the individual insurance market, so many coverage-loss paths remain open [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it protects a specific group of people — those with expensive, long-running conditions — from having coverage cut off mid-treatment. The cost, spread across all group plan enrollees through premiums, is harder to pin down, and the bill offers no estimate of it. Its small-employer exemption keeps the cost off the smallest firms but leaves many workers in small businesses unprotected. The omission of a cost estimate is a genuine design weakness, though the Institute of Medicine study would at least generate usage data.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the bill on March 5, 2008 [S1] [S5].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S5].
No further action was taken in the committee or on the floor before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and employers offering group coverage keep the ability to set lifetime caps on what they must pay, which limits their exposure to very high claims. Workers whose catastrophic care would have outrun a cap gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers keeping lifetime caps

for.name: Byron Dorgan
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Dakota; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate HELP Committee; it gained no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so there is no record of a party split; it simply died in committee without opposition being recorded.

industries.note: The bill would cap their ability to limit total lifetime payouts per enrollee, exposing them to more of the cost of very expensive medical conditions. Insurers face no recorded pressure either way in this bill's record, which shows no committee action at all.

Employers with 20 or more workers would face a higher floor on lifetime benefits they fund; the bill gives employers with fewer than 20 employees an opt-out, shifting the cost question away from small business.
